title: Why this program
intro: No randomized trial has ever compared pull-up progression schemes head to head. Linear plans, rep ladders, and rest-pause protocols have simply not been tested in controlled studies on pull-ups.

This program is a synthesis built from indirect evidence: training frequency, weekly set volume, rest between sets, proximity to failure, autoregulated progression, and eccentric loading for beginners. Every design choice below is tied to published research, and all sources are listed at the end of the page.
Where the evidence comes from bench press, lat pulldown, or squat studies, we say so. Those transfers are extrapolations, not proven facts about pull-ups.

overview.title: How the program works
body: You begin with a max-rep test. The result becomes your anchor M*, the app's estimate of how many strict pull-ups you can do in a single set. Every workout has five sets. A cycle has six workouts, and each workout is one step with slightly higher targets than the previous one.

Sets 1 to 4 are submaximal: fixed rep counts at 50 to 70% of the anchor. Set 5 is a maximum-effort set with a minimum rep count that rises from step to step. Hit every target and you advance to the next step. Miss any set and you repeat the same step next time.

The anchor updates after each completed cycle and again at a formal retest every four weeks. At the default three sessions per week, this adds up to 15 hard sets [1][2]. One set per workout goes close to failure and provides the progression signal [3][4]. Advancing depends on actual performance, not on the calendar [5][6].

levels.title: Entry test and levels
body: On your first session you do strict pull-ups to failure. The count is M. If M is zero, you enter Path 0 with eccentric and assisted work. Otherwise the app stores M as your anchor M* and assigns a level.

Levels are display labels for the statistics screen. They never change the math. M = 0 maps to Path 0, M from 1 to 4 to L1 Beginner, M from 5 to 9 to L2 Base, M from 10 to 19 to L3 Intermediate, and M of 20 or more to L4 Advanced.
The label only helps you read the progress charts. Set targets always come from the generator rule and your current anchor, never from the level name.

algorithm.title: Step generator: session(M*, k)
body: The app stores no fixed workout tables. Every step is computed from your anchor M* and the step index k, which runs from 1 to 6 within the current cycle.

Working sets 1 to 4 are ceil(0.7·M*), ceil(0.6·M*), ceil(0.6·M*), and ceil(0.5·M*), each at least 1 rep. Set 5 is of type Maximum with a minimum of N_k = min(ceil(0.6·M*) + k - 1, M* + 1). The cap at M* + 1 means a single step never asks for more than one rep above your tested max.

Example with M* = 7 and k = 3: working targets are 5, 5, 5, 4, and the final-set minimum is N_3 = min(5 + 2, 8) = 7. Reference tables for M* = 3, 7, 15, and 25 appear in the formulas section at the end of the page.

progression.title: Success, failure, deload, and retest
body: Success means all five sets meet their targets and the final set reaches N_k or more. The next scheduled workout is step k + 1.

Failure means any working set falls short or the final set lands below N_k. The same step repeats on the next workout. Two consecutive failures on one step trigger a deload: the anchor becomes floor(0.9·M*), minimum 1, and the same step is recalculated from the lower anchor. Autoregulated loading performs at least as well as fixed progression in meta-analyses [5], and other reviews find no downside [6]. Trained lifters commonly deload about every five to six weeks [7].

After six successful steps the cycle ends. The new anchor is M*' = max(best final-set reps in the cycle, M* - 1), and a new cycle starts at step 1. Every two cycles, about four weeks at three sessions per week, you run a full max test and its result becomes the new M*. Repeated max tests do not inflate strength gains on their own [8]. After a break longer than two weeks, the app suggests a retest or an anchor cut of roughly 10%.

frequency.title: Frequency: 3 sessions per week, 48 hours apart
body: The default schedule is three non-consecutive days per week, for example Monday, Wednesday, and Friday. Sessions must be at least 48 hours apart.

Training a muscle group twice per week beats once per week for hypertrophy in meta-analysis [9]. For upper-body strength, three or more weekly sessions beat one when volume is matched [10]. After a session that lowers strength by no more than 20%, strength is usually restored within about two days [11].
Two sessions per week is a valid option, especially at advanced levels when progress stalls. ACSM guidelines recommend training every major muscle group at least twice per week [12].

volume.title: Volume: 5 sets × 3 workouts = 15 per week
body: Each workout has five sets. Three workouts per week make 15 hard sets for the pulling muscles.

For strength, at least 10 sets per week clearly beat five or fewer, with an effect size of 0.18 [1]. For hypertrophy in trained lifters, 12 to 20 weekly sets per muscle is the commonly cited optimum [2]. A lat-pulldown trial found that five sets beat three and one on both strength and rep tests [13].
Fifteen weekly sets sit inside that range without reaching the zone of diminishing returns [14]. Volume helps up to a point, then gains flatten, especially for strength.

workingSets.title: Working sets: submaximal descending reps
body: The four working sets use descending fractions of the anchor: 70%, 60%, 60%, and 50%, rounded up. Most reps stay well away from deep failure.

One pull-up study compared stopping a set at 25% versus 50% velocity loss, and the earlier stop produced larger gains in strength and endurance [15]. Broader failure research shows that strength gains are similar across a wide range of reps in reserve [3]. Going to failure on every set costs reps in later sets and adds soreness [16].
Submaximal front sets preserve quality for the final max set. That is how you manage fatigue across a series of sets.

finalMax.title: Final set: maximum with a rising minimum
body: Set 5 is always a maximum-effort set with a floor of N_k reps. N_k rises by one each step until it hits the cap M* + 1. Over a full cycle the minimum typically climbs by three reps.

Muscle size tends to increase as sets end closer to failure, but the effect is small [3][17]. For strength, failure is not required [4][18]. Local muscular endurance gains look similar whether you stop at failure or two reps in reserve [19].

The exact package of four submaximal sets plus one max set has not been tested as a unit in a randomized trial. We assembled it from separate lines of evidence on volume, proximity to failure, and autoregulation. Treat that combination as an extrapolation.

rest.title: Rest between sets: 3 minutes by default
body: The default rest between sets is three minutes. Presets offer 90 seconds and five minutes, and you can adjust in 15-second steps during a workout.

For strength work at 50 to 90% of max, three to five minutes of rest allows more reps across multiple sets than short rest [20]. Trained lifters need more than two minutes to maximize strength gains [21]. In one squat study, one-minute rests cut reps from 7.7 to 2.2 by set four, while five-minute rests held them at 7.4 to 4.7 [22].

For hypertrophy, the benefit of resting beyond 90 seconds is unclear. A 2024 Bayesian meta-analysis found no meaningful difference above 90 seconds [23]. A 2025 preprint argues that long rest does not beat short rest for hypertrophy, though it still favors long rest for strength [24]. Since our goal is rep-max performance, three minutes stays the default. Path 0 uses 90 seconds to three minutes between sets.

path0.title: Path 0: starting from zero pull-ups
body: If your max test comes back zero, you follow a 12-step path in three phases of four workouts each, at three sessions per week.

Steps 1 to 4: scapular pulls, three sets of eight, plus hangs, three sets starting at 20 seconds with five seconds added each step. Steps 5 to 8: negative pull-ups, three sets with a three to five second lowering, plus assisted pull-ups, three sets of six. Steps 9 to 12: negatives, three sets of six, plus assisted pull-ups, three sets of eight. Then you retest and enter L1 if you can manage at least one rep.

Eccentric training has the strongest evidence for building strength when your concentric max is limited [25][26]. Eccentric-only work beats concentric-only work for eccentric strength, but concentric strength needs concentric practice too [27]. In one 12-week trial, a program with controlled eccentric tempo raised the pull-up max from 2.1 to 7.8 [28]. Scapular pulls and hang progressions have no direct RCTs. Those phases come from coaching practice and are marked as extrapolation.

skips.title: Missed workouts and returning after a break
body: Skipping a scheduled day neither advances nor penalizes your step. The missed workout stays available, and later dates shift forward by the gap while keeping the same spacing between sessions.

Strength is maintained for up to about three weeks without training, then decay speeds up [29]. Adolescent athletes lost nothing after three weeks off [30]. A break of two weeks or less: resume the same step. A longer break: take a fresh max test or accept an automatic anchor cut.

In a large field experiment, flexible scheduling supported long-term exercise habits better than rigid time windows [31]. In relapse-prevention research, guilt after a missed session is linked to worse outcomes [32]. That is why the calendar marks skipped days neutrally, not in red.

rejected.title: Patterns we rejected
body: Daily high-frequency training without rest days conflicts with the recovery data. Strength typically returns within two days, so hard sessions should be at least 48 hours apart [11].

Very high weekly volumes without a deload or a performance gate run into the dose-response ceiling and raise the risk of overuse [1][2]. Rest-pause protocols have RCT support on bench press and curls, but not on pull-ups [33]. With a fixed bodyweight load, the main rest-pause benefit, more reps at the same external load, matters less.
The interface has no RPE or reps-in-reserve scale. Novices misjudge their reserve by more than one rep on average [34]. The app uses an objective pass or fail gate instead.

limitations.title: Honest limits
body: No RCT has tested this exact progression scheme in pull-ups. Most of the supporting evidence is transferred from other exercises or muscle groups.
The four-plus-one max-set structure, the hang and scapular phases of Path 0, and the skip-reschedule policy are project extrapolations, not replicated trial findings.

The literature disagrees on some details. Frequency at matched volume [9][35], autoregulation versus fixed loading [5][6], and long versus short rest for hypertrophy [23][24] all have conflicting papers. We picked conservative defaults aimed at rep-max gains and noted the disputes where they matter.
